title: The Central American Paradox — Eddie Would Go

u.El istmo vive entre modelos autoritarios: The isthmus lives between authoritarian models that succeed on security and fragile democracies that fail to contain violence.
u.Cuando el miedo vence a la libertad: cua: When fear defeats freedom: four elections that define the future of Central America
u.El 1 de febrero de 2026, Costa Rica elig: On 1 February 2026, Costa Rica elected Laura Fernández president with 49.2% of the vote. She promised an "iron fist" against organised crime. Weeks earlier, Bukele had visited the country and Chaves, the sitting president, had announced plans for a "mega-prison". The question now is whether Costa Rica will follow the Salvadoran model — what Levitsky and Ziblatt call "democratic erosion", the gradual weakening of institutions by elected leaders — or whether its institutions will be able to contain it.
u.Esta historia comienza en El Salvador, d: This story begins in El Salvador, where Nayib Bukele built the model of "punitive populism" (Pratt): security in exchange for democracy. In 2023, Guatemala rejected it by electing Bernardo Arévalo. In 2025, Honduras, under Xiomara Castro, returned to left-wing populism, which attempted reforms and failed. In 2026, Costa Rica elected a candidate promising to replicate elements of that model. Four elections, one question: can Central America be safe without ceasing to be free?
u.El giro autoritario tiene causas estruct: The authoritarian turn has structural causes. Central America inherited weak states: the civil wars (1960-1996) destroyed institutions; the Cold War financed militaries rather than police forces. The fragmentation of the Mexican cartels (2006-2015) displaced violence southwards. MS-13 and Barrio 18, deported from the US, filled the vacuum. Today 60% of the economy is informal, 43% of young people are neither studying nor working (ECLAC), and remittances (21% of GDP in El Salvador) finance consumption, not investment. Drug trafficking moves US$150 billion a year in the region — more than all public budgets combined. These states never had effective, efficient state capacity. Bukele did not destroy something that worked; he offered order where there was only a vacuum.
u.El Salvador: El Modelo que Seduce: El Salvador: The Model That Seduces
u.Para entender Centroamérica hoy, hay que: To understand Central America today, one has to understand Bukele. Between 2015 and 2022, homicides fell from 103 to 7.8 per 100,000 inhabitants (PNC). His popularity reaches 91% (CID-Gallup, 2024). He won re-election in 2024 with 84.6% of the vote, despite a constitutional prohibition.
u.Pero el precio: El Salvador tiene la tas: But the price: El Salvador has the highest incarceration rate in the world (1,600 per 100,000 inhabitants, according to World Prison Brief). Two per cent of the population is in prison. The state of exception has run through more than 30 consecutive renewals since March 2022. Human Rights Watch documents trials of 900 people simultaneously, without due process, thousands of arbitrary arrests and total opacity over more than 235 deaths in custody.
u.El \"Caso Catedral\" (El Faro, 2020) rev: The "Cathedral Case" (El Faro, 2020) revealed that the initial fall in homicides was due to pacts: the government negotiated with MS-13 and Barrio 18 to reduce killings in exchange for prison benefits and territorial control. In 2021, the US Treasury Department placed two officials close to Bukele on the Engel List because of these negotiations. Bukele first made pacts with the gangs and then used them as a pretext to destroy democratic checks.
u.La ONU — a través de la Oficina de la Al: The UN — through the Office of the High Commissioner (then led by Michelle Bachelet) — expressed constant alarm at the erosion of the rule of law. Bachelet specifically denounced the fact that state-of-exception measures had led to mass arbitrary detentions, torture and deaths in custody, warning that public security cannot trample the right to a fair trial. The UN notes that the suspension of constitutional guarantees and the lack of judicial independence are creating a model of "mass punishment" that ignores international human rights standards.
u.Para enero de 2026, cuando Rodrigo Chave: By January 2026, when Rodrigo Chaves invited Bukele to visit the site of Costa Rica's future "mega-prison", the message was clear: the Salvadoran model is no longer an isolated experiment. It is an export manual.
u.Guatemala presenta un contraste instruct: Guatemala presents an instructive contrast. On 20 August 2023, Bernardo Arévalo won with 58% in the run-off. No poll predicted it. The establishment tried to prevent him from taking office. Only US pressure (Biden threatened sanctions) and citizen mobilisation allowed it. Today he governs with a Congress in which his party holds 23 of 160 seats and an attorney general (Consuelo Porras, cited by the US for corruption) who pursues his government.
u.Guatemala tenía ingredientes para el aut: Guatemala had the ingredients for authoritarianism: 10.3 million people in poverty, endemic corruption (only 7% trust the Presidency, Latinobarómetro). Arévalo promised the rule of law, not an iron fist. But a year later the results are ambiguous: he has not managed to pass major anti-corruption reforms, and violence persists (a homicide rate of 17.3 per 100,000 in 2024). His approval fell from 73% (January 2024) to 54% (December 2024, Prensa Libre). The "institutional model" has yet to prove that it works against organised crime.
u.Guatemala representa una apuesta: que se: Guatemala represents a wager: that crime can be fought without destroying democracy. Arévalo promised to attack the corruption that enables organised crime, strengthening institutions rather than concentrating power. But it is early to celebrate. His government faces systematic obstruction: no legislative majority, a corrupt prosecutor, no control over the police or the military. If Guatemala manages to reduce violence under these conditions, it will demonstrate that the institutional route is viable. If it fails, it will reinforce Bukele's argument.
u.En noviembre de 2025, Nasry Asfura del P: In November 2025, Nasry Asfura of the National Party defeated Salvador Nasralla by 515 votes. Days earlier, Trump (newly re-elected in the US) had pardoned Juan Orlando Hernández, the former Honduran president extradited for drug trafficking in 2022. The pardon was a message: the national establishment is protected.
u.El caso hondureño expone una verdad incó: The Honduran case exposes an uncomfortable truth: rejecting authoritarianism in favour of populist democracy guarantees neither democracy nor the republic. Castro came to power in 2022 promising to refound Honduras. She managed to reduce homicides to 19.5 per 100,000 inhabitants (the lowest level in thirty years). But governing against the structures of power is different from winning elections against them.
u.El Congreso bloqueó las reformas de Cast: Congress blocked Castro's reforms. Accusations of nepotism eroded her credibility. When Asfura won by 515 votes, Castro alleged fraud. The OAS certified the results, but local analysts note irregularities (Equipo de Reflexión, Investigación y Comunicación). Under pressure from Trump (who publicly backed Asfura), Castro handed over power on 27 January.
u.Lo que revela Honduras es la trampa del: What Honduras reveals is the trap of reformism without real power. Castro won the presidency but never controlled the state. The judicial apparatus, Congress, the economic elites, the military — all remained intact and hostile, recalling the attempts of her husband, former president Zelaya, to entrench himself in power. The result was the return of the National Party: the same party as Juan Orlando Hernández, extradited for drug trafficking and pardoned by Trump a few weeks before the elections. The pardon was a message: impunity is back.
u.Estas cuatro elecciones plantean la preg: These four elections pose the central question: can there be security without democracy? El Salvador says yes; Costa Rica will try to have both; Guatemala wagers that without democracy there is only tyranny. History favours Guatemala: authoritarian regimes that promise security end up failing on both fronts. But Bukele seduces because he works today: safe streets, children in schools, commerce without extortion. The cost — the destruction of the republic — will be seen when it is too late.
u.Bukele expone la contradicción de la der: Bukele exposes the contradiction of the Latin American right. It has criticised Venezuela, Nicaragua and Cuba for their authoritarianism, yet celebrates Bukele. The difference: Bukele delivers what the right values (order, punishment, markets) while suppressing what it claims to defend (checks and balances, a free press).
u.El dilema real es más profundo: ¿cómo de: The real dilemma is deeper: how does one defend liberal institutions when they do not provide basic security? The Salvadoran mothers who send their children to school without fear are not thinking about the long term, while they recover peace and calm, the value of their lives and the possibility of getting on without emigrating. They are grateful to be alive. It is understandable that defending the regime that failed them feels alien. Guatemala offers an institutional alternative, but has yet to show that it can reduce violence. Until it does, the Bukele model will go on seducing.
u.Ningún país ilustra mejor esta encrucija: No country illustrates this crossroads better than Costa Rica.
u.Costa Rica siempre fue diferente: sin ej: Costa Rica was always different: without an army since 1948 and with respected democratic institutions, spared the civil wars and internal conflicts that ravaged the rest of the region in the 1970s and 1980s.
u.Pero en 2025 registró 873 homicidios (ta: But in 2025 it recorded 873 homicides (a rate of 16.7 per 100,000 inhabitants), the third most violent year in decades. Blackouts and deteriorating infrastructure created the breeding ground for Rodrigo Chaves.
u.Chaves llegó al poder en 2022 con un 43%: Chaves came to power in 2022 with 43% abstention. Laura Fernández, his former minister, won with 49.2%. Bukele's visit weeks earlier was calculated propaganda. CID-Gallup reported that 34% arrived at the polls undecided.
u.La victoria de Laura Fernández en Costa: Laura Fernández's victory in Costa Rica is particularly worrying because the country is (or was) different. If Costa Rica falls into authoritarianism, there will no longer be exceptions in Central America. There will no longer be proof that "another path is possible".
u.Pero Costa Rica aún no ha caído. El Trib: But Costa Rica has not fallen yet. The Supreme Electoral Tribunal maintains its independence. The press is free. Civil society is organised. The question is not whether Costa Rica has tools with which to resist — it has them. The question is whether it will have the political and social will to use them.
u.Hay señales preocupantes. Chaves prometi: There are worrying signs. Chaves promised to appoint Fernández as a minister when he won; she promises to appoint him to her cabinet. This arrangement suggests that Fernández may not be the leader of the project but its presentable face — and that Chaves will remain the real power. And Chaves does not hide his contempt for institutional counterweights, his belligerence towards critical media, his explicit admiration for Bukele. The question is not whether the Fernández/Chaves pairing will try to replicate the Salvadoran model. The question is whether Costa Rican institutions will be able to stop it.
u.Escenario 1: Costa Rica resiste. Fernánd: Scenario 1: Costa Rica resists. Fernández implements professional police reforms. The TSE blocks attempts to concentrate power. Violence falls moderately. Costa Rica demonstrates that democracy and security are compatible, weakening Bukele's model regionally.
u.Escenario 2: Costa Rica cae gradualmente: Scenario 2: Costa Rica falls gradually. With popular support, Fernández obtains exceptional powers. By 2028, Costa Rica replicates El Salvador: mega-prison, mass trials, a silenced press. Panama and the Dominican Republic look on and consider the same road.
u.La historia de Centroamérica en 2023-202: The story of Central America in 2023-2026 is the story of four elections and four roads:
u.<span class=\"country-label\">El Salvado: El Salvador chose security without democracy. Impressive results today, catastrophic tomorrow. When Bukele falls or finishes, he will leave a country without institutions.
u.<span class=\"country-label\">Guatemala<: Guatemala chose democracy with uncertainty. Arévalo promises slow institutional construction. If it works, it will prove that crime can be fought without destroying republics.
u.<span class=\"country-label\">Honduras</: Honduras chose the return. Asfura restores the system Castro tried to dismantle. Lesson: rejecting authoritarianism with left-wing populism does not guarantee democracy.
u.<span class=\"country-label\">Costa Rica: Costa Rica will try to have both. It is the most seductive and most dangerous road. One cannot serve two masters: either you defend institutions or you capture them.
u.Por primera vez en su historia moderna,: For the first time in its modern history, Costa Rica faces the temptation that consumed El Salvador: the promise that a strong leader can solve what institutions could not. Laura Fernández will take power with a mandate for an "iron fist". What she does in the first hundred days will define the future of Costa Rican democracy. If she builds mega-prisons and declares states of exception, she will have chosen Bukele's road. If she strengthens a professional police force and respects institutional checks, she will have shown that another path is possible. The region is watching. Because if Costa Rica falls, there will no longer be exceptions. We shall see whether, as the cardinal warned, fear governs better than the legitimate weapons of the state.
